segments.text: To take an n-th root, divide the staircase. The angle of c has a name for every full turn. Divide each of those names by n and you get n different polar addresses. Take the length to the power one over n, and those are your roots.

Try the fifth roots of one. The names of its angle are zero, three hundred and sixty, seven hundred and twenty degrees, and so on. Divide by five: zero, seventy-two, a hundred and forty-four, and on up. Five dots, seventy-two degrees apart, all on the unit circle. Step five gives three hundred and sixty degrees, which is step zero again.

Now the fourth roots of minus sixteen. It has length sixteen and home angle a hundred and eighty degrees. The fourth root of sixteen is two. The angles are forty-five, a hundred and thirty-five, two hundred and twenty-five and three hundred and fifteen degrees. In Cartesian, each root is plus or minus root two, plus or minus root two times i.

Check one in polar. Length two, to the fourth power, is sixteen. Angle forty-five degrees, times four, is a hundred and eighty degrees. Length sixteen at a hundred and eighty degrees is minus sixteen. It works, and so do the other three.

The quadratic formula is a square root in disguise. For z squared minus four z plus thirteen, complete the square: z minus two, squared, equals minus nine. The square roots of minus nine are plus and minus three i. Slide by two, and the roots are two plus three i and two minus three i.

The principal root is the one on the home step. Two i has length two and home angle ninety degrees. So its principal square root has length root two and angle forty-five degrees. In Cartesian, that is one plus i. The other root, minus one minus i, comes from the next step up.
